projects.title: LUMA
projects.desc: Smart home prototype with two ESP32 boards running MicroPython: curtain control, keypad access, environmental sensing and ventilation, coordinated through MQTT.

detail.intro: A connected home, built at scale. Two ESP32 nodes bring sensing, access control and everyday automation into one physical prototype.
detail.overview: LUMA connects the physical and digital sides of a miniature smart home. One ESP32 manages the entrance, while a second controls the curtain and ventilation. Both run independent MicroPython applications and exchange commands and telemetry through MQTT, with Node-RED providing the dashboard in the original prototype.

approach.title: Two independent nodes
approach.text: Separate door and curtain applications keep each board focused on its own sensors and actuators. Device wrappers, control logic and communication modules have distinct responsibilities.

approach.title: Control through MQTT
approach.text: Commands and telemetry pass through a broker, connecting the physical model to a dashboard without combining both board applications into one firmware.

approach.title: Thresholds with hysteresis
approach.text: The curtain uses separate upper and lower thresholds for light and temperature, reducing repeated switching near a single boundary.

approach.title: Feedback at the entrance
approach.text: Keypad input, ultrasonic presence sensing, an OLED display and a servo make the access-control sequence visible on the model.

detail.outcome: The resulting scale model brings together sensor readings, actuator movement and remote commands. It remains an educational prototype: actuator operations are blocking, communication uses plain MQTT and access relies on a demonstration PIN. Non-blocking control and stronger communication security are natural next steps.
detail.credits: Team: Francesco Apicella, Luigi Autorino and Emanuel Chirico. Photographs and technical details from the LUMA repository.

projects.title: Aequitas
projects.desc: Verifiable e-voting prototype with RSA-OAEP encryption, Shamir secret sharing and ballot inclusion receipts based on Merkle trees.

detail.intro: An academic exploration of digital voting: encrypted ballots, shared trust and individual proofs of inclusion.
detail.overview: Aequitas is an academic e-voting prototype built around a separation of responsibilities: voter authentication, encrypted ballot submission, ballot registration and tallying. It explores how cryptographic primitives can work together to make a voting process inspectable.

approach.title: Encrypted preferences
approach.text: RSA-OAEP protects ballot preferences before they are submitted to the ballot register.

approach.title: Distributed trust
approach.text: Shamir secret sharing splits the election key across trustees, requiring a threshold of shares for reconstruction.

approach.title: Inclusion receipts
approach.text: Merkle-tree proofs allow a voter to check that a ballot is included in the register.

detail.outcome: The prototype combines a Flask application with an inspectable cryptographic workflow. Google OpenID Connect acts as a stand-in for SPID during authentication. This is an academic proof of concept, rather than a deployed election system.
detail.credits: Team: Luigi Autorino and Emanuel Chirico. Summary based on the project README.

projects.title: VibeFlow
projects.desc: Desktop music player with a track library, playlists and interchangeable playback modes, built as a JavaFX team project using Command, Observer and State patterns.

detail.intro: A desktop music player used to explore how software architecture supports a changing, interactive application.
detail.overview: VibeFlow is a JavaFX desktop application for managing a music library, building playlists and playing tracks. The project uses familiar music-player interactions to put software design patterns into practice.

approach.title: Reversible operations
approach.text: The Command pattern records actions on the library and playlists to support undo.

approach.title: Playback behaviour
approach.text: State models player states, while Strategy provides interchangeable sequential, shuffle and loop modes.

approach.title: UI coordination
approach.text: Observer keeps interface elements updated when application state changes.

detail.outcome: The application brings library management, manual and automatic playlists, playback modes and undo into one desktop interface. The repository also includes project documentation and team development artefacts.
detail.credits: Team: Luigi Autorino, Emanuel Chirico, Chiara Crisci and Emanuela Graziuso. Summary based on the project README.

projects.title: SafeStep-XR
projects.desc: Hackathon project simulating industrial emergency shutdown procedures in virtual reality, with guided sequences, timers and immersive interactions.

detail.intro: An immersive training prototype for industrial emergency procedures, built during the Youbiquo hackathon.
detail.overview: SafeStep-XR uses Unity and C# to simulate emergency shutdown scenarios in virtual reality. Guided actions, time limits and feedback let the user move through a simulated industrial emergency.

approach.title: Guided procedures
approach.text: The scenarios combine sequential tasks, timers and visual guidance for activities such as isolation, cooling and evacuation.

approach.title: Immersive interaction
approach.text: XR interactions bring scenario selection, equipment manipulation and navigation into the virtual environment.

approach.title: My contribution
approach.text: Initial menu logic, supporting scripts, general integration and bug fixing, as documented in the team README.

detail.outcome: The hackathon prototype demonstrates procedural training in a simulated environment. Repeated-session reset and return navigation are among the improvements identified by the team.
detail.credits: Team project developed during the Youbiquo hackathon. Contribution summary based on the repository team table.

projects.title: Waste Sorting AI
projects.desc: Eight-class waste image classification with ResNet18 and ResNet50, exploring transfer learning, data augmentation, oversampling and fine-tuning.

detail.intro: Teaching a neural network to recognise eight waste categories, and exploring what changes when the training strategy changes.
detail.overview: This machine learning project compares ResNet18 and ResNet50 for waste image classification. The eight categories are battery, clothing, glass, metal, organic, papery, plastic and undifferentiated waste.

approach.title: Transfer learning
approach.text: Pretrained ResNet models provide the starting point for classification experiments.

approach.title: Training experiments
approach.text: Oversampling, data augmentation and fine-tuning are compared across the two network architectures.

approach.title: Reproducible materials
approach.text: Notebooks, trained weights, dataset notes and a project report document the experiments and evaluation.

detail.outcome: The repository provides training and inference notebooks, final ResNet50 weights and an alternative ResNet18 checkpoint. Training was written for Google Colab and requires adapting the dataset and export paths before rerunning.
detail.credits: Team: Luigi Autorino, Emanuel Chirico and Alessio Ferrara. Summary based on the project README.
